claims.text: The as-cast HEA is initially a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
Service-relevant high-strain-rate loading causes localized nanoscale compositional instabilities in the initially single-phase HEA.
The loading-induced instabilities may take the form of segregation or nucleation of brittle intermetallic precipitates.
Nanoscale compositional deviations or precipitates hinder dislocation motion.
Intermetallic or secondary phases can increase strength while reducing ductility.
High-strain-rate local stress concentrations induce atomic mobility and short-range segregation.
Mechanical deformation can induce a phase transformation in an HEA.
Loading-induced microstructural changes create embrittled regions that lower ductility and cause premature brittle fracture.
Loaded samples will exhibit localized compositional fluctuations or newly formed brittle intermetallic phases detectable by TEM and EDS.
Loaded samples will have lower ductility and more brittle fracture features than the pristine baseline.
The pristine as-cast baseline has high toughness and ductile fracture behavior.
The proposed behavior is limited to significant mechanical loads at high strain rates and relevant operational temperatures.
Two sets of nominally comparable samples will be compared: unloaded as-cast controls and samples subjected to high-strain-rate tensile or impact loading.
Both groups will receive identical TEM/EDS microstructural analysis, mechanical-property assessment, and fracture-surface analysis.
The hypothesis is falsified if loaded samples remain homogeneous and single phase and show no statistically significant change in toughness or fracture behavior relative to the baseline.
